Right? So, in our high schools and middle schools, when you have one School Safety Agent or two School Safety Agents, is-- I'm just asking, is it feasible for them to complete all of-- just these

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 41 Committee on Public Safety four tasks, not anything else that was testified, for just these four tasks that you testified to?

Something that we have instituted, and I kind of want to make myself clear, maybe I should have said that at the beginning, we have instituted something called-- we started this school year's administrative rollout. School Safety Agents are basically assigned to require administrative positions within patrol boroughs and support units around-- go out on a daily basis to backfill for vacancies as you mentioned. Yes, people call out sick. You know, there are a lot of School Safety Agents who have kids and so on. They may have childcare issues. But that's the backfill. Those are the School Safety Agents we are utilizing to backfill absences and to assist with morning entry, dismissal, and everything else that is going on in the schools. And in addition to that, we also have a mobile task force assigned to every borough that will assess those schools where you might have one School Safety Agent with everything that they have to do.

On average, how many schools--is more-- how many agents call out in a day?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 42 Committee on Public Safety
That information, I don't have it with me right now, but I could definitely get back to you on it.

Because what you're describing sounds nice, but it just doesn't align with the experiences of the School Safety Agents at schools, or the principals or the teachers who say they are assigned nine agents at a school, but they typically have seven or six on any given day. Do you have data to shed light on how many absences? What are the vacancies on any given day? Because the mobile units do not make up for that, that's just not the experience of the principals and the teachers and the School Safety Agents who are doing the work on the ground.
I would like to get back to you on that once I pull that information.
Will you have it today?
Not today.

There's no one at the NYPD who can search up their data right now while council members are asking questions?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 43 Committee on Public Safety I mean, look, I don't doubt your desire to keep our kids safe. No one does. But I do doubt some of the testimony you've given in these 10 minutes about how there are no vacancies in our schools there. That School Safety Agents don't have one School Safety Agent for over 1,000 kids. That is just what is happening — that multiple School Safety Agents, due to forced overtime, are taking their comp time and taking off a day or two a week. Good for them, they have that time off. But to pretend that these vacancies don't exist and that mobile units are making up for it just isn't in line with the experiences of our school system.

We are acknowledging that the vacancies are there; obviously, they do exist. The numbers don't lie. However, the amount of vacancies has not deviated from School Safety Agents-- I mean, School Safety Division from our mission of keeping our schools safe.

I'm not questioning your mission, as I just said. I'm questioning whether you have enough School Safety Agents on any given day, not to mention the number of vacancies you have.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 44 Committee on Public Safety But besides that, on any given day, you have schools with over 1,000 kids in them with a single School Safety Agent. And I'm not sure if your data is wrong or if you're not being told what's happening in our schools. But that's what's happening in our schools, and it is leaving our kids at risk. And I don't even want to single--I don't think you do either, I don't think you want a single incident for any of our kids — and this is making our students less safe.

Chair, please, I welcome you to refer those specific cases to me. I'm heavily involved in everything that happens in school safety, and that is from not just communication with DOE, but also with principals. I have made it my business to visit schools, to talk to principals. And yes, I mean, I completely understand where you, you know, obviously, where you're coming from, all the information that you're getting, but I would like to speak on the untold stories and the stuff that doesn't come on the news that I deal with on a daily basis. And those are the emails from principals thanking me for the great work that School Safety is

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 45 Committee on Public Safety doing. The visits that I've done, where principals are praising a School Safety Agent, the Superintendents who are actually visiting schools in Brooklyn, praising agents for the work that they are doing. These are the untold stories– the School Safety Agent who, actually, a couple of weeks ago in Brooklyn, saved a kid from choking. They are in our schools, and we're doing our job.

Have not met a single principal who doesn't love their School Safety Agents. According to School Survey data, 83% of our students value our School Safety Agents. This isn't a question of whether we value them. The question is whether resources-- if there are enough resources so we can have more of them, if they're being deployed properly, if they're able to keep our kids safe. Because we know they do. We value them just the same.
But...

So that's not a question of whether or not we value them. Are they being deployed? Are there enough of them? And I want to go back to my original question. Does the NYPD have any minimum ratio? Not one per school, but if a school has a certain square footage or a school has a

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 46 Committee on Public Safety certain footprint or a school has a certain number of students where they hit a number and they say, all right, you need two, now you need three, now you need four School Safety at...
Absolutely.
minimum... (CROSS-TALK)
Absolutely, that’s why, what you... (CROSS-TALK)
What is that ratio? (CROSS-TALK)
When I-- I did answer your question, and I stated that the deployment of School Safety Agents to schools was based on student population. That comes into play, scan... (CROSS-TALK)
Thank you.
Scanning status. So yeah, absolutely. You know, that’s the type... (CROSS-TALK)

Let's break it down. In a population, what is the ratio of, let's say, there's no scanning, student to School Safety Agent ratio? What is it?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 47 Committee on Public Safety
Well, depending on the student population, as I mentioned, you might have schools... (CROSS-TALK)
Okay...
that has a 1,000... (CROSS-TALK)
For example, if there are 500 kids, how many School Safety Agents in general, without scanning, would they get with 500 students in a school?
Well, in a school, let's just say if it's not-- if it's not a high school, a supervisor and maybe three or four School Safety Agents.
Three or four School Safety Agents for 500? What about a high school of 3,000 kids? What would-- without scanning, what would that be? How many school Safety Agents... (CROSS-TALK)
You would probably get between 1:8 and one in 1:10.

Between 1:10 for a 3,000-student school?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 48 Committee on Public Safety Okay. And what if they're scanning at that school? How many School Safety Agents... (CROSS-TALK)
It all depends on the setups that we have at the school. Some schools might take one setup or two setups.
And for each setup, how many School Safety Agents are there?
You have three.
Three, right?
Yes.
Okay, so if you're-- I'm just doing a little math...
No, no, no...

I can't help it. I taught it. So if there are three scanners. Let's say there are three scanners and 3,000 kids — three times three is nine, plus one, you said, for 3,000 kids, there's a minimum of one. So, at a minimum, for 3,000 kids, there should be 10 assigned there. Is that the math?
Yes.

Okay.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 49 Committee on Public Safety

And obviously, that is coupled up. I said, yeah, you have those. But as I mentioned, we have the mobile task force, we have the Admin who goes out every day to support those schools with a large number of students with morning entry, dismissal, and everything that they have-- I mean everything else that they might need.

Okay. And then I just want to-- I'm going to turn it over to my co-chair in a second, and then to Council Member questions. But I do want to ask about the training and project PIVOT. Because they are both important. You mentioned in, Mr. Rampersant, you mentioned in your testimony about — NYC Public Schools contribute two weeks of training to the NYPD's 20-week School Safety Agent training program. This is a training that they get-- I want to make sure that the restorative justice is what is required in your training, or is that-- or is that just one of the things they may get trained on?

The Restorative--the Restorative Practices-- Restorative Practices is something that was newly added to the training of the

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 50 Committee on Public Safety School Safety Agents. I would say for the last maybe five or six school safety classes, we've been training School Safety Agents in Restorative Practices.
And is there any continuing education requirement for School Safety Agents in de-escalation tactics or in Restorative Justice, or problem solving techniques?

One of the things that we ask our schools to do is try to incorporate the School Safety Agents and the trainings that are done at the schools, uh, schools that are doing the restorative work with true fidelity. They're training school staff, and we try to-- well, we ask that they don't absent school safety from those spaces. One of the things that we've... (CROSS-TALK)
Is it-- you asked them or are they required?
They're not required. They are inviting the School Safety Agents to those trainings, right? We have what... (CROSS-TALK)

Can you just talk a little bit about the decision? I don't mean to interrupt, but I really want to get to this, you

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 51 Committee on Public Safety know, School Safety is dealing with very high stress situations in some cases... (CROSS-TALK)
Absolutely.

And so can you tell me more about the decision not to require continuing de-escalation training for School Safety Agents when it's wrapped into the Professional Development days, let's say that where there are no students in the school?

Absolutely, and I appreciate that question. One of the things that I want to make perfectly clear is we can't mandate School Safety Agents to do anything, right? We don't directly supervise the School Safety Agents. So that's why I use the term “invite” School Safety Agents to participate in training offered by school staff.
Who can mandate them?
The Police Department?

Okay. How are you doing? So we have a situation here where I'm just asking the School Safety Agents to get a ton of

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 52 Committee on Public Safety training, and they're fantastic, and they're also under a lot of stress. And there's no requirement that they do any--even every few years, some sort of de-escalation or sort of Restorative Justice refresher. The DOE offers it, but it's not required. Can you talk more about the requirement versus the suggestion?
Well, obviously, as part of our training, we focus on de-escalation. Our de-escalation training includes, uh, crisis de-escalation, conflict resolution.
Right.
youth mental health... (CROSS-TALK)

and I value all of that, and it's really important, and I understand the training. What I'm asking is about any sort of refresher course for School Safety Agents who are-- It's one thing to get the training, it's another thing to experience it on the ground when you're scanning people day in day out, getting in the middle of fights. Can the NYPD require or mandate any sort of refresher course, and do you?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 53 Committee on Public Safety
We...
Okay, you do...
We do that already.
And how often do you do that?
Usually, we try to utilize the times when school is off to bring everybody in.
And is that in conjunction with the NYPD or is that straight from the sorry-- is that in conjunction with the DOE or is that straight from the NYPD?
No, that's something that we do our, you know, that we do ourselves. So we take the initiative to do that at our own training unit... (CROSS-TALK)
And then... (CROSS-TALK)
Chair, if I may?
Yes, please.

So one of the things that we did to help double down on the training for the School Safety Division is we've trained their trainers, right? So all of their school safety

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 54 Committee on Public Safety trainers participate in an 11-day training on Restorative Practices. And so the Fundamentals of Restorative Practices, School Safety is doing sort of their annual training for all of their School Safety Agents. So this is the first year that it has been done in conjunction with New York City Public Schools. But we definitely did have their folks trained to continue to turnkey the training.
And so now, in the years going forward, there's an annual training for School Safety Agents on Restorative Justice and De-Escalation Practices? Is that what I'm hearing?
That is correct.

Okay. That's good. The last--with the plan and then to project PIVOT. There's training beyond-- there’s training beyond Restorative Justice and De-Escalation. There are large concerns about non-local law enforcement, namely ICE, being around schools, coming into schools. When was the last time that guidance was updated for the schools? And to what extent are School Safety Agents required to be trained on the guidance for non-local law enforcement?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 55 Committee on Public Safety
We instruct our School Safety Agents not to engage. The protocol is that if anyone from ICE agents...
You can ICE, yeah...
An ICE agent comes into the school, we immediately report, obviously we inform and notify the principal, and that's the extent of our involvement.

Good afternoon, Chair. Deputy Chief Thomas Alps, the Executive Officer of Patrol Services Bureau. Our policy was updated in January of 2025, and it strictly states that we don't assist or engage in Civil Immigration Enforcement. And then the policy states, should an officer encounter a federal agent engaging in Civil Immigration Enforcement, there's notification up the chain of command to a Deputy Chief who would then consult with our Legal Bureau and give guidance on how to proceed forward.

Thank you. And have New York City Public Schools updated their guidance as well? Or, when was the last time New York City Public Schools updated their guidance?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 56 Committee on Public Safety

So the New York City Public Schools guidance is ongoing. It's updated, you know, regularly. As a matter of fact, there are some changes coming to policy now. I can get you a more definitive answer as it relates to what has changed with the existing policy. I do have one of my colleagues here to speak about the existing policy and what we have done and continue to do to ensure that our young people are safe in our buildings.
I'm going to swear you in. Are you ready?
(INAUDIBLE)

You can do whatever you're comfortable with as long as you raise that right hand; it's up to you. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before these Committees and to respond honestly to Council Member questions?
I do.
Thank you.

Good afternoon, Members. My name is Kevin Dantzler. I am the Senior

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 57 Committee on Public Safety Director in the Office of Safety and Prevention Partnerships in New York City Public Schools. With respect to non-local law enforcement, as a general proposition, I want to state from the outset that New York City Public Schools does not consent to non-local law enforcement gaining access to school buildings or facilities. However, should there be a visit by non- local law enforcement, all school staff have been trained and advised that a School Safety Agent is to contact the principal and/or designee, a leader in the school, and have that non-local law enforcement agent wait outside. As you heard in our beginning marks, there's a door locking system where folks don't gain access unless they're being admitted by the door-- a (INAUDIBLE) access system. So the agent is to wait outside the premises. This principal and/or designee is to greet that officer, obtain the reason for their visit, get their name, their credentials, and, in the event there's some official documentation by way of court order, subpoena, warrant, and get that information and take that information and contact Senior Field Counsel.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 58 Committee on Public Safety Every single school in New York City public schools is supported by Senior Field Counsel. That documentation is to be transmitted to Senior Field Counsel for their review to ensure that it is valid. In the event that documentation is not valid, the principal and/or designee is advised that they should not allow non-local law enforcement to enter the building. They are to refuse entry. However, in the event that documentation has been verified as being valid, of course, all of our personnel are advised to comply with lawful subpoenas and/or court orders.

Thank you. I just want to make you aware that there was an incident before dismissal, a principal had verified ICE presence near the school building. When the principal escalated, there was no clear guidance for that kind of situation. They were unclear if they could call a shelter-in-place-- shelter-in, especially since it was a co-located campus. I'm going to leave it there. I do want to come back to this, and I have a number of other questions, and so do my colleagues, about ICE specifically, and about your

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 59 Committee on Public Safety Restorative Justice Practices. But I want to turn it over to my co-chair, Chair Feliz, for his line of questioning. And thank you for your answers to the question, although the Deputy Chief has one more answer.

Thank you for the opportunity. I just kind of want to clarify, and I forgot to mention that, obviously, at the beginning of the school year, when I was assigned as a School Safety Division Commanding Officer, I did an assessment of the personnel. And over 100 School Safety Agents who had been assigned to administrative duties were put back in schools. That was definitely one of the things that I instituted and helped us to reinforce the deployment at schools. So I'm sorry that I didn't say that... (CROSS-TALK)
Thank you for doing that. Thank you.
I wanted to clarify that because that makes a big difference.

Thank you. Thank you.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 60 Committee on Public Safety Chair Feliz?

Thank you, Chair Dinowitz. I'll focus first on School Safety Agents, and then I'll ask about school crossing guards. We want to know what's going well, and we, of course, want to know areas that need additional attention. Many questions about recruitment and retention of School Safety Agents, also budget-related needs, safety-related incidents in schools and outside the school, the scanning equipment being used, including how effective it is, and much more. As mentioned earlier today, in my opening statement, the staffing shortage is having real negative, detrimental consequences for our students and our school communities, including students being made late to class due to the batch systems that we have in place. And also speaking about the staffing shortage, we've had many, many, many conversations with School Safety Agents. We've heard directly from them, and they stated that there's very low morale in the Division for many reasons, including being underpaid, understaffed, feeling undervalued, and

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 61 Committee on Public Safety also having to unnecessarily travel long distances with very little to no notice. And of course, I'm not a School Safety Agent. I don't have any personal knowledge of that. But given the high turnover that continues to exist, I think the high turnover rate speaks volumes on the points that they're making on that. So I'll start with some basic questions. What is the budgeted headcount for School Safety Agents? How many vacancies do we have? How many open positions are there?
Our authorized head count is 4,065, with the actual head count of 3,915. As I mentioned earlier during my testimony, our current vacancy is 360.

Okay, 360. And speaking about the long lines that I mentioned earlier, due to the lack of safety agents, is this something that you have heard about? If yes, how often does that happen? Long lines around the schools because there's not enough School Safety Agents to scan the...

Well, this is obviously the first time I've heard about this. Feel

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 62 Committee on Public Safety free to let me know if there are any specific schools or any other incidents that you might have heard about, you know, please bring them to my attention. I'll be more than happy to look into it. But I'll start by explaining what the scanning protocol looks like for us on a daily basis. Basically, our scanning process starts obviously, before the start of-- before the kids get to school. We do have, as I mentioned, special services which are basically support units that deal with scanning, supporting many of our scanning schools throughout the city, and we've relied on our mobile task force, which we have one per borough, to assist with morning entry, and expedite the scanning at schools.
Okay, so you've never heard about students being made late to class due to the fact that there are not enough School Safety Agents to scan the items?
No.

Okay, that's actually very interesting because my principals are very vocal, especially about this issue, when they've been reaching out repeatedly to the School Safety Office.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 63 Committee on Public Safety So you're not knowing that information, that's interesting to say the least. Uh...

Well, I speak through e-mail with many of the principals if there's any issue. But one of the things that we're doing is that, you know, I'm like, as I mentioned before, very heavily involved with everything that goes on with school safety. So we address issues as they come in real time. And that's not only what I'm doing, but it's what I'm expecting from everybody else under my leadership.
What about the Department of Education? Is the Department of Education aware of any lateness caused by the staffing shortage or due to not enough School Safety Agents?

So thank you for the question. Obviously, it's an ongoing issue as it relates to the shortfall. It is definitely being felt throughout the school system, as you just indicated in conversation with principals. It is something that our folks on the floor are dealing with directly with

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 64 Committee on Public Safety principals, and they deal directly with commanding officers. And as the Chief continues to share her personal experiences with these notifications, one of the key responsibilities for people on the floor is to make sure that that information doesn't make it to, you know, hierarchy. So these are, in many cases, things that are dealt with at the lowest level.

Talk to us about some of the stories that you've heard from educators and parents, and students on this issue. How late? What's the worst incident that you've heard where students are made late to class?

I think the worst incident that I've heard is a scanning machine breaking down, and that's the school that requires more than one scanning mechanism, which means that we have to now rely on a single machine. This particular incident was quickly remedied, but just think about going through an airport, and if they delay one person, that backs up another person. So the most I've heard is a machine that broke down, and that was quickly remedied, but the

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 65 Committee on Public Safety time frame by which it takes sometimes causes the backup.

And you could get back to us if you don't have the information in front of you, but approximately how many students did that school have? And also, how late were the students made to class? Are we talking about 10 minutes? Half an hour?
Yeah, I can definitely get back to you with this particular school.
But do you have a ballpark of how late the students were made to class?

No, right? Because this is not a single session in school, right? So there are students who have a first period, and there are students who have a second period, right? Depending on where you are on the line is going to determine whether or not you're late for your class or early for your class, right? Students with the second period, who come to school early, may just be on time for their second period class, while students in the first period may be later. So I have to get back to you.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 66 Committee on Public Safety

Yeah. So, if you don't have the information on this incident, that's fine. But, do you have any knowledge of any schools or any information on how late the students were made for any incidents related to lateness due to the lack of School Safety Agents?
Due to the lack of School Safety Agents?
Or insufficient, they call out, or the equipment breaks down?

Yeah, yes, I appreciate the question. I don't know the timeframes by which young people are late, because I'm not focused on how late they are. I'm focused on whether or not students are late and what we can do to remedy the problem, right? So my focus is always on getting the people on the floor to mitigate some of what we're experiencing at a particular school.

Thank you for the information. I also want to recognize Council Members Lee and Krishnan, who have joined us.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 67 Committee on Public Safety How is retention in this division, in the division related to SSAs and ASSAs?

We are very proactive when it comes to our retention efforts, and I would take the best way to describe it, uh, I'll start by saying that our priority or main focus is to keep morale up. Obviously, you want to make sure that the School Safety Agents assigned to our division feel valued. I'm making it my business, or we make our business at all levels, to ensure that the work that they are doing is being acknowledged. How do we do that? Obviously, through issuing Commander’s Days. We also do school visits, where I personally, myself and my staff, thank them for just being there, for being themselves in the role that they play in the safety of our schools. We have training opportunities, we have scholarship opportunities, as I mentioned in my testimony. We encourage them to advance; we encourage career advancement among the different ranks of School Safety. We also do discretionary promotions from Level I to Level III, which is a supervisory promotion for them. Another component of our retention efforts is peer support. We have a

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 68 Committee on Public Safety dedicated group of peer support staff who work in conjunction with the NYPD and the Employment Assistance Unit to provide counseling and guidance, and emotional support to our School Safety Agents. Obviously, they are there for everybody else, so I have to make sure that we are there for them. The Peer Support Units also follow up on members who are long-term sick, those members who are injured in the line of duty, and so on. And that’s the-- obviously, pay equity, we want to ensure that available and voluntary overtime, their salary and earnings are up to-- so they can be up to par in comparison with other civil service titles.
Can you just repeat the budgeted head count, the actual head count on the vacancies? Is it 4,065 budgeted headcount? Actual headcount approximately 3,900?
Yeah, well, I'm sorry, let me just rephrase that. In all ranks, it is 4,065; for School Safety Agents, it’s 3,915.
That's the budget headcount?

Yes, for School Safety Agents.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 69 Committee on Public Safety
And there are approximately 360 vacancies?
Yeah, 300 and (UNINTELLIGIBLE) 55.
How long have those positions been vacant for? And also, what's the average tenure? How long do these School Safety Agents last in the division?
Chief, if I may?
Yes...
So, looking at payroll data, I found out that roughly 75% of the School Safety Agents are at top pay, meaning five years or more.
Okay. How many schools are currently operating with fewer SSAs than their assigned allocation?
I don't have that information with me, but I could definitely get back to you on that.

Approximately how many-- what's the average-- on a daily basis, how many School Safety Agents do we have that haven't,

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 70 Committee on Public Safety for example, called out and et cetera, because we're hearing that that's an issue as well?
Roughly 20%, per borough... (CROSS-TALK)
Roughly 20%?
